claims.original_text: Students who sleep at least seven hours perform better on examinations.
claims.rationale: The results excerpt reports that the at-least-seven-hour group had a higher mean examination score than the less-than-six-hour group, and that the adjusted association remained after controlling for age, year of study, and self-reported employment hours. The design excerpt confirms a cross-sectional survey with sleep duration and examination score collected during the same end-of-term questionnaire. The claim is worded as an associational group comparison, which matches the evidence.
claims.revised_text: Students who sleep at least seven hours perform better on examinations.

claims.original_text: Getting at least seven hours of sleep improves examination performance.
claims.rationale: The evidence supports only an association: the results excerpt reports a higher mean score in the at-least-seven-hour group and an adjusted association, but also states no random assignment or longitudinal follow-up was performed. The design excerpt confirms a cross-sectional survey with sleep and examination score collected at the same time. The causal verb 'improves' exceeds what this cross-sectional design can support.
claims.revised_text: Getting at least seven hours of sleep is associated with better examination performance.

claims.original_text: The finding applies broadly to university students because the adjusted association was robust.
claims.rationale: The results excerpt supports an adjusted association, but the design excerpt notes the sample was recruited from two campuses, and the limitations excerpt states that two-campus sampling and the single examination outcome limit population-wide interpretation. Claiming broad applicability to university students overstates the generalizability of the evidence.
claims.revised_text: The adjusted association was observed in this two-campus sample of university students, but the finding may not apply broadly to all university students.

limitations: Two-campus sampling limits generalizability to the broader university student population.
Self-reported sleep duration is subject to recall error.
The study used a single examination outcome, limiting the scope of the performance measure.
Residual confounding may remain despite adjustment for age, year of study, and self-reported employment hours.
content.revised_summary: A cross-sectional survey of 1,248 university students found that students reporting at least seven hours of sleep had higher average end-of-term examination scores than those reporting less than six hours, and this association remained after adjustment for age, year of study, and self-reported employment hours. Because the design was cross-sectional with no random assignment or longitudinal follow-up, the evidence supports an association rather than a causal effect of sleep on examination performance. Interpretation is further limited by two-campus sampling, recall error in self-reported sleep, a single examination outcome, and residual confounding.
